summary: Defines extension header formats for the Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE), RFC 4326, and for the Generic Stream Encapsulation (GSE) used in second-generation Digital Video Broadcasting systems. These extensions let IP traffic over broadcast links carry extra information, such as optional fields. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Satellite TV signals can also carry internet data in small packages. This paper defines extra labels you can stick on those packages for added information.

subtitle: Three extra headers for ULE and GSE that carry MPEG-2 packets, bundle small packets, and add timestamps.

tldr.problem: ULE and GSE carry IP over MPEG-2 and second-generation DVB links, but lacked ways to send MPEG-2 control packets, to pack many small PDUs efficiently, or to measure link timing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three Extension Headers: TS-Concat (type 2) carries MPEG-2 TS Packets, PDU-Concat (type 3) packs several PDUs into one SNDU, and TimeStamp (type 257) adds a 32-bit time value.
tldr.outcome: The extensions share one IANA ULE Next-Header Registry and work in both ULE and GSE, giving both a common way to do these jobs.

facts.label: TS Packet size used in length check
Maximum length of one concatenated PDU

today: RFC 5163 is a Proposed Standard from April 2008. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Context: ULE, GSE and Extension Headers
sections.content:
The Unidirectional Lightweight Encapsulation (ULE, RFC 4326) carries IP over links using the MPEG-2 Transport Stream. Generic Stream Encapsulation (GSE) is the equivalent for the Generic Mode of second-generation DVB physical layers, first for DVB-S2. Both wrap a PDU in an SNDU (SubNetwork Data Unit).

In ULE, a Type field value below 1536 decimal marks an Extension Header, and GSE uses the same Type semantics. GSE differs in having no CRC per SNDU, different header flags and a different length calculation. This RFC defines three such extensions, usable with both.
sections.plainLanguage: ULE and GSE put internet data into little envelopes for sending over broadcast links. Extension headers are extra labels on the envelope.

sections.title: Header Ordering
sections.content:
The RFC gives a recommended order for Extension Headers inside one SNDU, from first to last: link framing and transmission fields (the TimeStamp Extension), then headers working on the whole remaining payload (an Encryption Extension), then headers for a group of PDUs (PDU-Concat or TS-Concat), then headers for a specific PDU (an IEEE-defined type, Test or MAC bridging Extension).

This does not mean all types appear in one SNDU. It is a guideline that may help receivers process headers efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: When you stack stickers on an envelope, there is a sensible order so the person opening it can read them one by one.

sections.title: TS-Concat: Carrying MPEG-2 Packets
sections.content:
The MPEG-2 TS-Concat extension has H-Type 0x0002 and is a Mandatory Extension Header. It carries one or more MPEG-2 TS Packets in a ULE SNDU, for example MPEG-2 SI/PSI signalling. GSE has no native TS Packet support, so it gives GSE an MPEG-2 control plane.

The number of packets is found from the payload size. With no other extensions and D=0, it is (Length-10) / 188. For GSE the equivalent is (Length-6) / 188. A receiver MUST check that the length is a whole number of TS Packets. If not, it MUST discard all encapsulated packets and SHOULD record a TS-Concat size mismatch error.

NULL TS Packets SHOULD NOT be sent this way. The encapsulator SHOULD have a bounded, configurable TS Packing Threshold, the longest time it waits before sending queued packets. A larger value can improve efficiency but adds jitter and could raise the chance of corruption. Carrying clock references such as the Network Clock Reference raises timing issues the RFC does not address.
sections.plainLanguage: This sticker says 'inside are TV-control packets, all exactly the same size'. The sender waits a short time to fill the box, but never too long.

sections.title: PDU-Concat: Bundling Small PDUs
sections.content:
The PDU-Concat extension has H-Type 0x0003 and is a Mandatory Next-Header Extension. It sends a sequence of usually short PDUs in one SNDU payload. It suits many small PDUs for one NPA address, and can cut duplicated MAC layer overhead. A receiver not configured for that NPA address can skip many PDUs in one operation.

The extension has a 16-bit PDU-Concat-Type. All concatenated PDUs MUST share one Type, and PDU-Concat cannot be nested. Each PDU is prefixed by a length, with a reserved most significant bit R that MUST be zero and that receivers MUST ignore. Each PDU length MUST be less than 32758 bytes. PDUs need not be 16-bit or 32-bit aligned. In ULE with D=0, one 6-byte NPA address applies to all PDUs. With D=1 there is no NPA address.

Like TS-Concat, it uses a bounded, configurable PDU Packing Threshold. The receiver checks the PDU-Concat Type (discarding unsupported types, recording a PDU-Type error), verifies each PDU length and that the lengths sum to the base header Length. Otherwise it SHOULD discard the SNDU and record a PDU-Concat size mismatch error. It MUST NOT forward a partial PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of mailing ten tiny letters in ten envelopes, you put them in one big envelope with the length of each letter written in front of it.

sections.title: The TimeStamp Extension
sections.content:
The TimeStamp extension has H-Type 257 decimal and is an Optional Extension Header. It supports monitoring and measuring link performance. The RFC lists possible uses: validating in-sequence ordering per Logical Channel, measuring one-way delay (with synchronized clocks), measuring PDU jitter, and measuring PDU loss with extra information from the sender.

It carries a 32-bit value at 1 microsecond resolution, counting ticks past the hour in Universal Time when the PDU was encapsulated. This may be earlier than the actual transmission time because of packing and queuing. Systems that cannot reach that resolution MUST pad unused least-significant bits with zero. A final 16-bit Type field gives the payload type or a further Next-Header.

Receivers MAY process the TimeStamp, and may skip it, but MUST continue processing the rest of the SNDU and forward the PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: This sticker records the time the package was packed, so someone can later work out how long the trip took.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA assigned three Next-Header Type values in the ULE Next-Header Registry: 2 (TS-Concat), 3 (PDU-Concat) and 257 (TimeStamp, H-LEN 3). TS-Concat and PDU-Concat are Mandatory, TimeStamp is Optional.

Security considerations for ULE are in RFC 4326 and RFC 4259. An attacker able to inject arbitrary TS Packets into a ULE or GSE stream may modify layer 2 signalling carried by TS-Concat, but this needs access to the link or layer 2 equipment, and such an attacker could equally attack native TS signalling. Address resolution and signalling issues are covered in RFC 4947.
sections.plainLanguage: A person who can slip fake packets onto the link could confuse the TV-control messages, but they would first need to get onto the link.

sections.title: Appendix: Second-Generation DVB
sections.content:
The appendix explains the DVB-S2 setting. Second-generation DVB offers more efficient physical-layer methods with adaptive coding and modulation, and more flexible framing, including the Generic Stream alongside the classical Transport Stream.

A DVB-S2 link multiplexes baseband frames (BBFrames), each with a fixed-size 10B header and a payload. A stream is a sequence of BBFrames sharing an Input Stream Identifier, and each stream is an independent link. GSE offers ULE-equivalent functions. It uses the LT field in place of ULE's D field, and the S and E flags for flexible fragmentation, with a CRC-32 in the last fragment.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer satellite systems pack data in flexible boxes called frames, and GSE is a way to fit internet packets into those boxes.
